descricao: Hair types, colors and styles; body and skin vocabulary; modifiers (quite, fairly, rather...); grooming phrases.

secoes.conteudo:
Here is a situation you probably know. Your friend is waiting for you at a busy coffee shop, and they call: 'I can't find you! Where are you?' You say 'I'm here!' That does not help. 'I'm the person... with a face...' Still nothing. What you need is the right vocabulary — words to describe what you look like, fast and clearly.

Describing appearance is one of the most practical skills in any language. We use it to find people in a crowd, to describe someone we just met, to remember someone from a long time ago. In English, this vocabulary comes up all the time — in conversation, in films, in books, everywhere.

In this unit, you will learn two main things. First, the words to describe hair, skin, and body type. Second, how to make those descriptions sound natural — not just 'she is tall' but 'she is quite tall' or 'he is fairly slim.' Small words that make a big difference. Let's start.

Hair is usually the first thing we notice about a person. And in English, we can be very specific about it.

The first thing we describe is **hair type** — the shape of someone's hair. **Straight** hair falls flat and smooth, with no waves or curls. **Wavy** hair has soft, gentle curves — think of the letter S, and you have the idea. **Curly** hair has tight, round spirals. If you have ever seen a phone cable from the 1990s, that is the shape of very curly hair. These three words — **straight**, **wavy**, and **curly** — are the most important ones for hair type, and you will hear them constantly.

Then we have **hair length**. **Long**, **short**, and in between — simple enough. There is also a useful word for a hairstyle: a **ponytail**. This is when long hair is tied together at the back of the head. It is a very specific image — the moment someone says 'she had her hair in a ponytail,' you know exactly what she looked like.

Now for **hair color**. **Dark** hair means brown or black — it covers a wide range of darker shades. **Blonde** hair is light yellow or golden. **Fair** hair is similar to blonde and is often used to describe very light-colored hair, especially in British English. And one more: **grey** hair, which comes naturally with age. Some people prefer to call it **silver**, which sounds a little more elegant — and honestly, it is.

One important word: **fair**. As we said, **fair** hair means light-colored hair. But **fair** is also used for skin — **fair skin** means light or pale skin. So 'she has fair hair and fair skin' means everything is light. This word works for both. Keep it in mind — it comes up a lot.

Now let's talk about body type and skin. This vocabulary is very useful for descriptions, and there are some important differences between similar words.

For body shape, the key words are **slim**, **thin**, **muscular**, and **overweight**. Here is something worth knowing: **slim** and **thin** both mean 'not heavy,' but they feel very different. **Slim** is almost always a positive word. It suggests someone looks healthy and in good shape. 'She is very slim' sounds like a compliment. **Thin** is more neutral — and sometimes it can even suggest concern, like someone has lost weight and looks unhealthily light. Native speakers choose **slim** when they want to be kind and positive. When in doubt, use **slim**.

**Muscular** describes someone with strong, visible muscles — like a person who exercises a lot. And **overweight** is the polite, neutral way to say someone is heavier than average. It is simply a description, without judgment.

For height, you already know **tall** and **short**. In real conversations, people almost always add a small modifier before these words — and we will look at those modifiers in the next section.

For skin, the most common adjectives are **pale**, **dark**, and **tanned**. **Pale** skin is very light — it does not get much sun. **Dark** skin describes darker skin tones. **Tanned** skin is interesting: it means light skin that has become darker because of sun exposure. It is not someone's natural color — it is a change from being in the sun. And in British English, you might also hear **spotty**, which means skin with spots or pimples. Teenagers know this word well.

secoes.titulo: A Little, Very, or Somewhere in Between? Modifiers
secoes.conteudo:
Here is the section that will make your English sound much more natural and real. Native speakers almost never say just 'she is tall' and stop there. They add a small word before the adjective to show how strong the description is. These words are called **modifiers**, and they are everywhere in real English.

The modifiers you need to know are: **really**, **very**, **so**, **quite**, **fairly**, **pretty**, and **rather**. Let's look at each group.

**Really**, **very**, and **so** make an adjective stronger. 'She is really tall.' 'He is very muscular.' 'Your hair is so curly!' These feel natural and common in everyday conversation. **So** in particular adds emotion. When you say 'so,' you mean it — you are a little surprised or impressed. 'She is so slim!' carries more feeling than 'She is very slim.'

Now the interesting ones: **quite**, **fairly**, **pretty**, and **rather**. These four words all soften an adjective — they mean 'not completely, but a significant amount.' They are all similar, but each one has its own personality.

**Quite** is the most common and neutral. 'She is quite slim' means she is slim, but you are being calm and measured. 'He has quite long hair' is a simple, polite observation. **Fairly** sounds a little more careful. 'She is fairly tall' means she is tall, but not unusually so. **Pretty** — and here is the important part — when used as a modifier, **pretty** has nothing to do with 'beautiful'! It simply means 'quite' or 'rather a lot.' 'She is pretty short' means she is noticeably short. This use of **pretty** is very common in American English, so you will hear it a lot in films and series. And **rather** sounds a bit more British and sometimes suggests a mild surprise. 'He was rather thin' feels like 'hm, thinner than I expected.'

Here are some real example sentences: 'She was quite slim.' 'He has pretty curly hair.' 'I am fairly tanned.' 'She was rather pale.' All of these sound completely natural. This is the kind of English that makes people think 'wow, your English is really good.'

Beyond describing how people look, we also need to talk about the things people do to change or take care of their appearance. This vocabulary is very useful in everyday life — and it also gives you good practice with the present continuous.

To **get a haircut** means to go to a hairdresser and have your hair cut short. 'I need to get a haircut' is a sentence you will hear and use all the time. To **brush your hair** means to use a brush to make your hair neat and smooth. To **comb your hair** is the same idea, but with a comb — the thin tool with small teeth, usually used for shorter or straighter hair.

To **shave** means to remove hair with a razor. Men often shave their face in the morning. 'He shaves every day.' To **put on makeup** means to apply cosmetics — things like foundation, lipstick, and mascara. 'She puts on makeup before work.' And to **get dressed** means to put on your clothes. 'I need to get dressed' might be the most common morning sentence in the English language.

All of these phrases work naturally in the present continuous — the form we use for actions happening right now. 'He is shaving.' 'She is brushing her hair.' 'They are getting dressed.' You already know this tense, so this is a great opportunity to use new vocabulary with a familiar structure. Two things at once — always a good deal.

Let's finish with a few words that are worth thinking about carefully — either because they have a similar word in Portuguese with a different meaning, or because they work differently from what you might expect.

First: **slim** and **thin**. In Portuguese, both of these translate to 'magro.' But in English, they are not the same. **Slim** = positive, healthy, attractive. **Thin** = neutral, sometimes a little negative. If you want to compliment someone, use **slim**. If you are describing that someone looks underweight or frail, **thin** is more appropriate. Choosing the right one shows a real understanding of English.

Second: **fair**. This word has many meanings in English, and appearance is just one of them. In appearance: fair skin = pale skin, fair hair = light-colored hair. But fair also means just or equal, as in 'It's not fair!' It can also mean good enough — 'The film was fair, not great.' And in weather: 'a fair day' means clear and pleasant. You will see this word in many different contexts. Do not be confused — just look at the situation.

Third: **dark**. When we describe appearance, **dark** is the natural, polite, and common word for hair or skin in darker shades. 'She has dark hair.' 'He has dark skin.' It is simply a color description — neutral, clear, and widely used. Portuguese speakers sometimes look for a more specific word, but in English, **dark** covers a wide range and is always appropriate.

And finally: **tanned**. In Portuguese, you might say someone is 'bronzeado.' In English, **tanned** describes exactly that — skin that has become darker because of the sun. It implies the person spends time outdoors or on a beach. 'He looks very tanned' often sounds like a compliment in English — it suggests an active, outdoor lifestyle.
